name: Posture tracker wearable (Upright Go)

lead: The Upright Go is a small sensor worn on the upper back or neck. It buzzes when you slouch, and people use it to build a taller, more upright carriage that makes shoulders and neck look more open.

The chain is real-time feedback, then a corrected habit, then a more upright stance. It has been used in published ergonomics studies of surgeons' neck and back posture and in a small Parkinson's pilot; none of them measured appearance.

paras: It is worn during the day, often while sitting at a desk, and vibrates when posture drops past a set angle. Users typically pair it with back and core strengthening or mobility work, and wear it for a few weeks to build awareness before using it less.

No safety concerns are described in the studies found. It needs to be worn against the skin or on clothing, which some people find irritating. How much posture change lasts after the device comes off has not been well studied.

angle.text: Posture trainers like the Upright Go sit on the upper back and vibrate when you slouch, so you correct yourself in the moment and gradually build a more upright carriage. Clinician ergonomics studies have used the device.

lead: UpRight Go 2 is a commercially available wearable posture-training device that records neck and spine posture and provides biofeedback to prompt correction.[1] It is promoted for slouching, and the entry is discussed here as posture gear.

Published use is mainly in clinicians and small clinical groups: otolaryngology surgeons, ophthalmic surgery trainees and a pilot study in Parkinson's disease.[1][2][3] No study identified has examined it for physical appearance.

paras: A 2022 study recorded neck and spine posture of surgeons performing otolaryngology procedures with UpRight Go 2, first measuring baseline posture and then adding biofeedback to evaluate whether it improved ergonomics.[1] A 2023 study evaluated a posture trainer on trainee back posture during ophthalmic surgery.[2] A pilot study examined a wearable postural intervention called UpRight in Parkinson's disease.[3] Another study measured ergonomics in vitreoretinal surgery with a wearable device, and a 2026 study used biosensor technology to quantify cervical posture in microsurgery.[4][5]

Related biofeedback research includes a trial in 96 university students comparing electrotherapy, exercise, a biofeedback posture trainer and postural education.[6] No trial has tested the device for looks or in a general gear-buyer population.
